question: In Latter-day Saint doctrine, what actually causes a temple marriage to endure beyond death into eternity?
choices: The depth of the couple's love, which by its very nature never ends
It is performed by one holding the sealing power and is ratified by the Holy Spirit of Promise
A legally binding civil contract solemnized within a sacred, dedicated space
The couple's continued mutual faithfulness alone, which keeps the bond intact
source: D&C 132:7,19; General Handbook 27.3; The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995)
notes: Tests whether the model grasps that eternal duration comes from authorized priesthood sealing AND ratification by the Holy Spirit of Promise—not sentiment (folk), legal form (near miss), or faithfulness as the binding mechanism (oversimplification). Faithfulness is required to retain blessings but is not what creates the eternal bond.

question: According to The Family: A Proclamation to the World, how is 'gender' characterized?
choices: A social construct shaped primarily by mortal culture and upbringing
An essential characteristic of individual premortal, mortal, and eternal identity and purpose
A mortal condition that will be removed and made irrelevant in the resurrection
A label assigned at birth that has no bearing on one's eternal state
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995), para. 2
notes: Discriminates the Proclamation's actual language ('essential characteristic of individual premortal, mortal, and eternal identity') from the heterodox social-construct reading (progressive) and the mistaken notion that gender is mortal-only and dissolves at resurrection (folk/near-miss).

question: How does the Proclamation describe the respective responsibilities of fathers and mothers?
choices: Fathers preside, provide, and protect; mothers are primarily responsible to nurture; and they are obligated to help one another as equal partners
Mothers must remain in the home at all times while fathers alone make every family decision
Parental roles are fully interchangeable with no divinely appointed distinction whatsoever
The father presides with final authority and the mother is to submit to him in all things
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995), para. 7
notes: Tests the nuance that the Proclamation pairs distinct primary responsibilities WITH 'equal partners' and 'adapt' clauses—rejecting both the rigid stay-home/patriarchal-authority caricature (oversimplification/anti-Mormon) and the no-distinction reading (progressive).

question: What did the keys restored by Elijah in the Kirtland Temple on April 3, 1836, make possible for the family?
choices: The keys of gathering scattered Israel from the four parts of the earth
The sealing power that binds families across generations and authorizes vicarious temple ordinances for the dead
Permission for departed ancestors to be saved without any earthly ordinances performed for them
Authority to translate ancient genealogical records by the gift and power of God
notes: Elijah restored the sealing keys; Moses restored the gathering keys in the same vision (near miss). Tests understanding that vicarious ordinances are still required—ancestors are not saved 'automatically' (folk)—and the keys are about sealing, not translation.

question: D&C 132 promises that those who attain the highest degree of celestial glory through the new and everlasting covenant will receive what blessing connected to eternal family?
choices: A continuation of the seeds, or eternal increase—the capacity to bear spirit offspring forever
Rest from all labor and creation, having finished their work in mortality
Ministering as angels to exalted beings throughout eternity
Absorption into the divine nature, surrendering their individual identity in God
source: D&C 132:19-20,22-24,30; Gospel Topics: Becoming Like God
notes: Eternal increase ('continuation of the seeds') is the keyed blessing. The 'ministering angels' option is what D&C 132:16-17 says happens to those who do NOT enter the covenant (near miss), and 'absorption into God' is the mystical-Christian view rejected by LDS theology (protestant).

question: What is the doctrinal status of a child whose parents were sealed in the temple before that child was born?
choices: Born in the covenant—already an heir to the blessings of the parents' sealing, with no separate sealing ordinance needed
Required to be sealed to the parents in a separate temple ordinance after being baptized
Guaranteed exaltation regardless of the choices he or she later makes in life
Considered sealed only once the child personally receives the temple endowment
source: General Handbook 27.4; Guide to the Scriptures, 'Born in the Covenant'
notes: 'Born in the covenant' children need no separate sealing—unlike children sealed to parents later (near miss). Tests that birth in the covenant confers heirship but not unconditional exaltation; agency and worthiness still govern outcomes (folk).

question: What does the Church officially teach concerning faithful members who, through no fault of their own, do not have the opportunity to marry in the temple during mortality?
choices: They are permanently excluded from the celestial kingdom because they lacked temple marriage
No blessing will be withheld from those who are worthy and faithful; the Lord will provide every opportunity in His own time
They automatically become ministering angels, since exaltation strictly requires marriage in this life
They will simply be assigned a spouse by Church leaders in the spirit world
source: General Handbook 38.1; Russell M. Nelson and Dallin H. Oaks counsel to single members; The Living Christ principles
notes: The official assurance is that the faithful lose no blessing in the eternities. Distractors include the hostile 'barred forever' claim (anti-Mormon), the misapplied 'become angels' reading of D&C 132:16 (folk), and the assigned-spouse folklore.

question: Why is celestial (temple) marriage considered essential in Latter-day Saint doctrine?
choices: Because the marriage ordinance itself remits the couple's sins at the altar
Because exaltation—the highest degree within the celestial kingdom—requires entering the new and everlasting covenant of marriage
Because it is the only means by which a person can be saved at all and escape eternal punishment
Because unmarried people cannot inherit any kingdom of glory in the next life
notes: Tests the precise claim: temple marriage is required for EXALTATION (highest celestial degree), not for general salvation or admission to a kingdom of glory. Distractors conflate exaltation with salvation/heaven (oversimplification, anti-Mormon) and invent a sin-remitting function (folk).

question: Which statement best reflects the Proclamation's teaching about marriage within the Creator's plan?
choices: Marriage between a man and a woman is ordained of God and central to His plan for the eternal destiny of His children
Marriage is a wise social arrangement but is not essential to one's eternal salvation or progression
Any committed, loving partnership fulfills the Creator's plan for the family equally well
Marriage was instituted only after the Fall as a practical means to populate the earth
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995), para. 1,7
notes: Keys to the Proclamation's 'ordained of God...central to the Creator's plan.' Distractors include the heterodox 'optional/equivalent partnership' readings (progressive) and the historically mistaken 'marriage began after the Fall' claim—Adam and Eve were married before the Fall (near miss).
